title: Which Risk Is It?
blurb: The core skill: look at a bit of .NET code or a scenario and name which OWASP 2025 category it falls under. Sort each into its bucket — the legend explains them.

levels.title: L1 · The big three
levels.prompt: Sort each into the OWASP 2025 risk it represents.

items.label: Building a SQL string by concatenating Request.Query["name"]
GET /orders/{id} returns any order — no owner check
items.note: changing the id shows other users' data

items.label: Storing passwords hashed with MD5, no salt
A DB password committed in appsettings.json
Admin action with no [Authorize] and no role check

levels.explain: Input becoming code (SQL concat, @Html.Raw XSS) is Injection. Reaching data/actions you shouldn't (IDOR, missing [Authorize]) is Broken Access Control. Unprotected sensitive data (MD5 passwords, a committed secret) is Cryptographic Failures.

failStates.title: XSS is Injection
failStates.explain: Cross-site scripting is untrusted input rendered as executable script — that's Injection (A05), the same family as SQL injection. It isn't about permissions.

failStates.title: That's Broken Access Control
failStates.explain: No malicious input is being executed — the query is fine. The problem is it returns records the caller shouldn't see. Missing an ownership check is Broken Access Control (A01).

failStates.title: A leaked secret is a crypto failure
failStates.explain: Committing a password/connection string is failing to protect sensitive data — Cryptographic Failures (A04). Use User Secrets in dev and Key Vault / managed identity in prod.

levels.title: L2 · The subtler four
levels.prompt: Sort each scenario into its OWASP 2025 category.

items.label: A referenced NuGet package has a known CVE, years out of date
Repeated failed logins produce no log entry or alert
catch (Exception) { } wrapping an authorization check
items.note: the failure is ignored, code continues

items.label: Json.NET with TypeNameHandling.All on untrusted input

levels.explain: Trusting tampered data/code (BinaryFormatter, TypeNameHandling.All) is Integrity Failures. An outdated/vulnerable dependency is Supply Chain. No record of security events is Logging & Alerting. Swallowing an exception so a check is skipped is Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

failStates.title: Deserialization is an integrity failure
failStates.explain: BinaryFormatter on untrusted input lets an attacker craft an object graph that runs code — Software/Data Integrity Failures (A08). Supply Chain (A03) is about the packages you depend on, not the data you deserialize.

failStates.title: Swallowing an exception is A10
failStates.explain: An empty catch around an auth check means a failure is ignored and the code proceeds — Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions (A10, new in 2025). Logging & Alerting (A09) would be about not RECORDING the event, not about the control being skipped.
